claims.text: A conventionally synthesized Zr-Nb-Hf-Ta-Mo high-entropy alloy can form a single-phase, uniformly crystalline matrix.
Low-level Pt addition to Zr-Nb-Hf-Ta-Mo produces nanoscale localized amorphous or paracrystalline motifs within the crystalline matrix.
Heat treatment after Pt doping promotes local atomic rearrangement.
Pt has a large negative mixing enthalpy in the proposed alloy environment.
The negative mixing enthalpy associated with Pt promotes local atomic reshuffling.
Pt-induced atomic reshuffling generates amorphous or paracrystalline regions.
Localized amorphous or paracrystalline regions impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases alloy hardness.
Impeded dislocation motion increases yield strength.
Pt-doped Zr-Nb-Hf-Ta-Mo alloys will have greater hardness than identically processed Pt-free controls.
Pt-doped Zr-Nb-Hf-Ta-Mo alloys will have greater yield strength than identically processed Pt-free controls.
High-resolution microscopy will reveal localized amorphous or paracrystalline features in the Pt-doped alloys.
The localized disordered features will correlate with enhanced mechanical performance.
The identically processed Pt-free baseline has a homogeneous crystalline structure without localized disordered regions.
The proposed behavior is limited to Pt concentrations below the solubility limit.
The proposed behavior may not persist at higher Pt concentrations or in fundamentally different alloy systems.
A controlled test should vary low-level Pt content while keeping heat treatment and mechanical testing conditions identical to those of the Pt-free control.
